# Breakable Integrals

Also called: Distributable Integral Functions

## Overview
Breakable integrals are a family of integral functions defined over a domain $[t_1, t_{N+1}]$ that can be rewritten as a sum of products of integrals over individual segments $[t_k, t_{k+1}]$ [S1]. This decomposition enables the parallel or distributed computation of the total integral by allowing partial results from independent segments to be combined [S1]. Unlike standard parallel primitives that distribute data elements across threads, this family distributes the mathematical structure of the integral itself, making it suitable for multi-GPU implementations where segments are processed independently and aggregated [S1].

## Shared principles
Parallel execution principles are inherited from [Parallelism and Distribution](6265-parallelism-and-distribution.md). The mathematical mechanism common to this family is the decomposition of an integral over $[t_1, t_{N+1}]$ into a sum of products over segments $[t_k, t_{k+1}]$ [S1]. The general form is $\mathcal{F}(t_1 + t_{N+1}) = \sum_{i=1}^N \left( \prod_{j=1}^N H_{ij}(t_j + t_{j+1}) \right)$ [S1]. The family satisfies two closure properties: (1) multiplying, adding, or subtracting breakable integrals yields a breakable integral, and (2) integrating a breakable integral yields a breakable integral [S1]. Simple integrals like $\int f(t) dt$ are breakable with $H_{ij} = \mathcal{F}$, while complex coupled integrals may not be [S1]. Key examples include transmittance, where $T(t_1 + t_{N+1}) = \prod_{i=1}^N T(t_i + t_{i+1})$ [S1]; volume rendering, $C(t_1 + t_{N+1}) = \int_{t_1}^{t_{N+1}} T(t_1 + t) \sigma(t) c(t) dt$ [S1]; and distortion loss, $\mathcal{L}_{dist}(t_1 \rightarrow t_{N+1}) = 2 \int_{t_1}^{t_{N+1}} T(t_1 \rightarrow u) \sigma(u) S(t_1 \rightarrow u) du$ [S1].

## Subtopics

## Background
The concept of breakable integrals was introduced in the context of scaling Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) across multiple GPUs [S1]. The primary motivation was to enable efficient distributed training and inference by partitioning the ray integration domain [S1]. The family is characterized by its ability to decompose complex integrals into segment-wise operations that can be aggregated, facilitating parallel processing in distributed systems [S1].
